text: A message queue feeds three worker processes. When the queue backs up, the workers fetch bigger batches, which take longer to finish and let the queue back up further. A full test copy of the setup is available, and any load can be replayed against it as often as needed. Will doubling the incoming message rate make the backlog grow without limit?

A message queue feeds three worker processes. When the queue backs up, the workers fetch bigger batches, which take longer to finish and let the queue back up further. The change goes straight to the live system, nothing like it can be tested beforehand, and a backlog that builds up cannot be cleared without losing messages. Will doubling the incoming message rate make the backlog grow without limit?

Two scheduled jobs on one server each lock table A and table B, one taking A first and the other B first. Their start times are fixed and their past durations are logged to the second, but tonight's durations will vary slightly. An exact replica of the server is available, and tonight's schedule can be replayed on it as often as needed. Do the jobs deadlock tonight?

A log file grows by 2 GB a day on a disk that has 40 GB free. Nothing else writes to the disk, and no spare machine exists on which to test anything. Is the disk full within three weeks?

A log file grows by 2 GB a day on a disk that has 40 GB free. Once the disk is more than 90 per cent full, the database on the same disk slows down, its requests start timing out, and every timeout writes a long error trace into that log. No spare machine exists on which to test anything. Is the disk full within three weeks?
